title: Akara
subtitle: West African black-eyed pea fritters
excerpt: Akara are Nigerian and Ghanaian fritters made from blended black-eyed peas. The skins are removed after soaking, the beans are blended into a smooth batter, and the fritters are deep-fried until crisp and golden. They are eaten for breakfast or as a street snack.
sourceNotes: Akara is eaten across West Africa and the African diaspora. In Brazil -- where it was taken by enslaved Africans -- it is known as acaraje and is a famous Bahian street food. The technique of removing the skins and blending the beans is the defining step.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The batter can be made and refrigerated for up to 24 hours. Fry just before serving.

content.text: Using tinned black-eyed peas speeds this up considerably. Drain and rinse them well, then rub them between your palms under cold water to remove the skins. The batter should be fluffy -- whip it hard with a fork to incorporate air before frying.

items.prepNote: use black-eyed peas (tinned, drained) -- rub off the skins under running water

content.text: Drain and rinse the black-eyed peas. Rub them between your palms under running water to loosen and remove the skins. Drain well.
Blend the beans with the onion, chilli, salt, and 3 tablespoons of water until completely smooth. The batter should be thick and hold its shape.
Beat the batter vigorously with a fork for 2 minutes to incorporate air. It should look slightly fluffy.
Heat the oil in a deep pan to 180 degrees. Drop tablespoons of batter into the hot oil. Fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until golden and cooked through.
Drain on kitchen paper. Serve hot with pepper sauce or pap (corn porridge).

items.symptom: Fritters fall apart in the oil
items.cause: Batter too thin or beans not blended smoothly enough
items.fix: Blend until completely smooth; add less water next time -- the batter should be very thick

items.cause: Oil too hot -- outside browns before inside cooks
items.fix: Keep oil at 180 degrees and fry for a full 4 minutes; do not rush by using higher heat
Beat the batter hard with a fork for at least 2 minutes before frying to lighten it

content.text: Akara is morning food across Nigeria and Ghana -- sold outside mosques after Friday prayers and at bus stations in the early morning. The African diaspora carried the recipe to Brazil, where acaraje from Salvador da Bahia is now a protected cultural heritage dish. The technique is identical; only the toppings differ.
